newsitem.title: INDONESIA: U.S. official says East Timor tense but sees hope.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official says East Timor tense but sees hope.

text.p: A top U.S. human rights official on Friday described the situation in East Timor as one of "considerable tension" but said a new United Nations initiative to reach a solution had sparked some hope.

John Shattuck, U.S. assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, said he concluded his visit to the Indonesia-ruled territory "with a sense of hope ... that the discussion of human rights and the future of East Timor can proceed to a new level."
Shattuck left East Timor's capital Dili earlier on Friday after a 24-hour visit to the former Portuguese colony, which was invaded by Indonesia in 1975 and annexed a year later.
There he met local government and military officials, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Bishop Carlos Belo, human rights activists and heads of non-government organisations.

Residents believe about 200,000 people were killed in the invasion, a subsequent famine and two decades of strife in which Indonesian authorities have sought to clamp down on a movement for independence.

"It (the situation) can proceed to a new level if Indonesia, Portugal, the international community and the people of East Timor all work together under the auspices of the U.N. secretary general," Shattuck told a news conference at Bali's Denpasar airport.
"East Timor is a place where people deserve to be able to speak much more freely than they now can about their own interests and their own future.

"The human rights climate is one of considerable tension but I'm pleased that in recent months there have been fewer cases of reported severe violence. We believe that that climate will be considerably improved if the dialogue that I've referred to and the commitment that the United States and other countries have to that dialogue is followed through."

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Anan last month appointed a special envoy for East Timor to speed the search for a solution to the future of the troubled territory. The envoy, Jamsheed Marker of Pakistan, is also in Indonesia on a familiarisation visit and is due to visit East Timor on Saturday.

Marker visited Lisbon earlier this month and said he hoped for a speedy resumption of U.N.-sponsored talks between Indonesia and Portugal to reach an internationally-acceptable solution on the future of East timor.
The bilateral talks have dragged on for nearly 15 years without resolution.

Shattuck said he visited Fernando do Araujo, an East Timorse political activist in custody since 1993, in a Jakarta jail and received assurances that he would receive medical attention for high blood pressure and a kidney infection.
The U.S. official said he had also received assurances that jailed labour leader Muchtar Pakpahan would receive all the medical attention that he required.

Pakpahan, on trial on subversion charges that carry a death sentence, was taken to hospital earlier this month for a biopsy on a tumour on his right hand. The results of the test have yet to be announced.
